description: Empire of Timur (Tamerlane) and his successors (1370–1507) based in Samarkand; extended from Anatolia to Delhi; famous for devastating campaigns against Delhi (1398), the Ottoman Empire (1402), and the Golden Horde; later Timurid rulers became major patrons of Persian art, architecture, and scholarship at Herat and Samarkand.

temporal.notes: Timur seizes Samarkand 1370; dies during campaign against China 1405; Timurid successors rule Transoxiana and Khorasan until Uzbek conquest 1507; Babur, a Timurid, founds Mughal Empire in India 1526

lifecycle_phases.description: Timur consolidates Transoxiana; devastates Iran, Iraq, Georgia, and the Golden Horde (1395–1396); sacks Delhi (1398); defeats and captures Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I at Ankara (1402); dies en route to China 1405

Timur's successors Shah Rukh and Ulugh Beg rule from Herat and Samarkand; massive patronage of Persian miniature painting, architecture, and astronomy; Ulugh Beg builds observatory measuring star positions; Islamic Golden Age in Central Asia

Internecine wars between Timurid princes; Abu Said defeated and killed by Aq Qoyunlu (1469); eastern territories lost to Uzbek Shaybani Khan by 1500; last Timurid Husayn Bayqara rules Herat until Uzbek conquest 1507; Babur flees west then to India

rise_factors.description: Timur was arguably the greatest military commander since Genghis Khan: his combined-arms tactics, use of psychological terror, and systematic destruction of enemies' economic bases overwhelmed all opponents
Timur faced a weakened Ilkhanate successor states, a divided Golden Horde, a declining Delhi Sultanate, and an Ottoman state still consolidating power in Anatolia, none could mount unified resistance
Though not himself a Chingissid, Timur ruled through puppet Chingissid khans and married into the family; his title "Guregen" (royal son-in-law) gave him legitimacy in the Mongol world
Control of Samarkand, the greatest entrepôt on the Silk Road, and the beautification of that city with looted artists and craftsmen gave the empire enormous revenues and prestige

decline_factors.description: Timur divided his empire among multiple sons and grandsons without a clear succession rule; internecine war began immediately after his death in 1405 and never fully ceased
The Uzbek confederation under Muhammad Shaybani Khan consolidated north of the Syr Darya and progressively conquered Timurid territories; Samarkand fell 1500, Herat 1507
Timur's devastation of Baghdad, Delhi, and the Golden Horde disrupted the very trade routes that funded his successors' patronage; the Silk Road's western branches remained weakened for generations
